passages.source: F01 · Local solar time of an overpass
passages.text: FIRMS stamps every fire pixel with the time in UTC. Fires, farmers and satellites follow the Sun, not Greenwich. This formula moves each detection onto the Sun's clock at the place where it was seen, so that a 13:30 pass means the same thing over Punjab, California and Córdoba. Three parts of FIREWORK depend on it. First, a fire cell-day (F05) must be a local day. A fire seen at 20:30 UTC over Punjab is already the next morning there; binning by UTC date would put it on the wrong

passages.source: F01 · Local solar time of an overpass
passages.text: already the next morning there; binning by UTC date would put it on the wrong day and, at month ends, in the wrong month of the calendar. Second, MODIS and VIIRS are compared by overpass. Terra looks in the late morning, Aqua and the VIIRS satellites in the early afternoon. Only on the solar clock do these windows line up the same way everywhere on Earth, so day and night strata (F13) and matched pairs (F20) can be built consistently. Third, the Blind Spot page asks what share of a

passages.source: F01 · Local solar time of an overpass
passages.text: (F20) can be built consistently. Third, the Blind Spot page asks what share of a day's burning falls inside the moments the satellites look (F45). That question only makes sense on the Sun's clock, because burning follows sunshine and field work, not UTC. Indian Standard Time is not a substitute. IST is pinned to 82.5°E, so over Punjab (about 74–77°E) it runs about 20–35 minutes ahead of the Sun. Using IST would shift every overpass by that amount. The formula is a shift and a wrap. passages.text: by that amount. The formula is a shift and a wrap. Converting acq_time 0748 to decimal hours gives $7 + 48/60 = 7.80$ h. Adding $\lambda/15$ moves the clock east or west. The modulo keeps the result between 0 and 24, so a detection at 23:00 UTC at 30°E becomes 01:00 the next local day. tex: t = 7.80 + \tfrac{75.74}{15} = 7.80 + 5.05 = 12.85\ \text{h} \;\Rightarrow\; 12{:}51\ \text{LMST} The local date is computed from the same shifted timestamp, not from the UTC date, so every daily and

passages.text: computed from the same shifted timestamp, not from the UTC date, so every daily and monthly aggregation downstream uses the day that a farmer at that spot would recognise. Apparent solar time would add $E(d)/60$ hours. FIREWORK bins detections into days and half-hour windows, where the 16-minute equation of time does not change any assignment except right at midnight, so the mean solar time is used and the apparent correction is documented, not applied. passages.source: F02 · Pixel footprint and scan-angle growth
passages.text: A fire pixel near the edge of a satellite swath covers far more ground than one straight below the satellite. This formula gives the real ground area each detection stands for, which explains why MODIS and VIIRS dots look so different and why one bigger pixel is not one bigger fire. FIREWORK compares counts from two sensors whose pixels differ by a factor of about six in area at nadir and by much more at the swath edge. Without this formula it is tempting to read the large MODIS squares

passages.source: F02 · Pixel footprint and scan-angle growth
passages.text: the swath edge. Without this formula it is tempting to read the large MODIS squares on a map as large fires. They are not: the footprint is the size of the observation, not the size of the fire inside it. The footprint also explains the exchange rate k (F11–F14). A small field fire covers a tiny share of a 1–10 km² MODIS pixel and may not raise its temperature enough to trigger detection, while it can fill a meaningful share of a 0.14 km² VIIRS pixel. That geometry is a

passages.source: F02 · Pixel footprint and scan-angle growth
passages.text: can fill a meaningful share of a 0.14 km² VIIRS pixel. That geometry is a main reason VIIRS reports more fire cell-days than MODIS for the same farms. Footprints are also the basis for sensitivity checks, for example repeating a calculation using only near-nadir MODIS pixels, and for the 'why the dots differ' explanation on Sensor Lab. For every detection the pipeline keeps scan and track exactly as FIRMS delivers them. The footprint is their product. No angle is needed because FIRMS has already solved the geometry, including Earth curvature.

Points from two sensors never fall on the same coordinates. To compare them, FIREWORK drops every detection into a fixed 0.1° grid that is the same for every sensor, every year and every region. This formula turns a latitude and longitude into that grid cell, robustly, even at exact cell edges. Every count on the site starts here. The fire cell-day (F05), the monthly count (F06), the cell areas (F04) and the region membership table all use the same cell_id. If two sensors used two grids, or if edge points

all use the same cell_id. If two sensors used two grids, or if edge points flipped between cells, the comparison between MODIS and VIIRS would carry an artificial difference that no calibration could remove. passages.source: F04 · Area of a grid cell on the sphere
passages.text: A 0.1° cell is not a fixed number of square kilometres: it is 124 km² at the equator and 106 km² over Punjab. This formula gives the exact area of a latitude–longitude cell on a spherical Earth, so densities and regional totals compare fairly between latitudes. Counts per cell mean different things at different latitudes. A cell over Córdoba (about 31–35°S) and one over Punjab hold roughly the same area, but cells over northern Canada are half as large. VIIRS draws many small dots over a burning village; MODIS draws a few big ones. Counting dots would compare pixel sizes, not fires. The fire cell-day asks one fair question of both sensors: was any fire detected in this 0.1° cell on this local day? The MODIS–VIIRS harmonisation is a comparison of two rulers. If the ruler were 'number of pixels', VIIRS with pixels about six times smaller would read several times higher for the same fire, and the ratio would mostly measure pixel size. With cell-days, both sensors answer

same fire, and the ratio would mostly measure pixel size. With cell-days, both sensors answer a yes/no question about the same 100 km² box on the same day, so the remaining difference is mainly what each sensor can detect (F20), which is exactly what the exchange rate k should capture. Keeping the platform and the day/night pass in the key matters. It lets FIREWORK fit separate day and night exchange rates (F13), match platforms with similar overpass times (Aqua with S-NPP), and later divide by the number of valid looks

similar overpass times (Aqua with S-NPP), and later divide by the number of valid looks of the same platform (F09). Detections that pass the quality rule (F07) and are not static industrial sources are grouped by cell, local day, platform and pass. Any group with at least one detection becomes a cell-day with value 1. Several revisits in a day by the same platform are merged on purpose; they are one opportunity on one day, not several fires. Alongside the flag, the table keeps how many detections formed it and

not several fires. Alongside the flag, the table keeps how many detections formed it and the maximum and summed fire radiative power, so nothing is lost for later analysis. Each platform contributes exactly one cell-day: $c = 1$ for S-NPP, NOAA-20 and Aqua. Each sensor grades its own detections, but in different languages: MODIS gives a number from 0 to 100, VIIRS gives a class, low, nominal or high. This formula keeps each sensor in its own language, applies one documented rule per sensor, and measures how much the answer depends on that choice. The exchange rate k is a ratio of two filtered counts. If the filter for one sensor is much stricter than the other, k changes even though the fires did not. FIREWORK therefore fixes one default rule per sensor

changes even though the fires did not. FIREWORK therefore fixes one default rule per sensor in its own language and publishes how k moves under other reasonable rules. That spread is part of the honest uncertainty of the harmonised record. It also keeps the user interface truthful: the confidence control on Explorer is a named rule, not a slider that pretends both sensors share one probability scale. The default keeps MODIS detections with confidence at least 30 and VIIRS detections of class nominal or high. The 30 threshold removes the

least 30 and VIIRS detections of class nominal or high. The 30 threshold removes the lowest-scored MODIS pixels while keeping almost all real agricultural fires; nominal + high is FIRMS's own recommended VIIRS default. For the sensitivity grid the pipeline recomputes Oct–Nov cell-days for both sensors under four MODIS thresholds and three VIIRS class sets and divides them. The default pair sits inside the grid, so a reader can see whether it is typical. In Punjab + Haryana the default rule keeps 97.0% of MODIS vegetation-fire detections and 87.7% of

Punjab + Haryana the default rule keeps 97.0% of MODIS vegetation-fire detections and 87.7% of S-NPP detections (classes: nominal 84%, low 12%, high 4%). For October–November cell-days, 2012–2025, the default rule gives k = 2.27. The eight rule pairs that keep nominal-class VIIRS and MODIS thresholds up to 50 give k between 2.24 and 2.50. A brick kiln, a gas flare or a steel plant is hot almost every day of the year. A rice field burns once. Persistence measures how often a site is seen hot out of the days it could have been seen, so steady industrial heat does not inflate the farm-fire calendar or the calibration. FIREWORK's calendar and its exchange rate are about vegetation and crop fires. A kiln that is detected on hundreds of days would add the same cell-days every month, raise quiet months and change k in ways

would add the same cell-days every month, raise quiet months and change k in ways that have nothing to do with agriculture. The live pipeline already drops detections FIRMS marks as volcanoes or static sources; persistence extends that to sites FIRMS has not catalogued. On the Sources page, persistence is one of the pieces of evidence for calling a site agricultural, industrial or uncertain, together with night share (F44) and context (F42–F43). The numerator counts days the site was hot. The denominator counts days the site could have been seen,

days the site was hot. Dividing by calendar days instead would make cloudy places look less persistent. When nothing was observable the score is unknown, not zero. A cloudy November and a quiet November can produce the same low count. Satellites cannot see fires through cloud, so FIREWORK divides the fire cell-days by the number of cell-days the satellite actually had a clear look. The result is burning per look, not burning per calendar day. Smoke and monsoon cloud are worst exactly when and where burning peaks. A raw count therefore undercounts the cloudiest months, and if cloudiness differs between years it can look like a trend. Dividing by exposure removes that artefact. Exposure is also the

can look like a trend. Dividing by exposure removes that artefact. Exposure is also the correct offset in the count model (F14). Comparing MODIS and VIIRS per valid look, instead of per calendar day, separates 'sees fewer fires' from 'had fewer chances to look'. On the Calendar the metric switch 'exposure rate' uses this formula; on the Brief it is listed as 'fire cell-days per valid day'. This is the formula that answers the challenge. MODIS months from before VIIRS existed are converted into VIIRS-equivalent units by multiplying by the exchange rate k for that calendar month. After 2012 the calendar shows what VIIRS actually observed. The 25-year record then sits on one ruler. passages.text: Day and night detection work differently. At night the ground is cool, so small fires stand out, and VIIRS's finer pixels see far more of them than MODIS. Mixing day and night into one exchange rate hides that. FIREWORK computes k separately for each pass, using the real overpass times. Night burning matters for FIREWORK in two ways: industrial sources burn at night (F44), and a shift of crop burning toward evening would move fires away from the afternoon passes (F45). Terra's morning crossing has moved earlier and Aqua's afternoon crossing later in recent years as their orbits decay. FIREWORK uses the observed acquisition times rather than nominal 10:30 and 13:30, so 'day' and 'night' strata are defined by what the satellites actually did. passages.source: F14 · Poisson GLM with exposure offset
passages.text: The exchange rate is best written as a count model: both sensors watch the same burning, each has its own sensitivity, and the number of looks enters as an offset. The model gives k as the difference of two sensor effects, and its simplest form is exactly the ratio of totals used on the live site. Writing k as a model, rather than just a ratio, does three things. It shows what is being assumed (both sensors see the same activity in a stratum). It allows exposure to enter properly,

passages.source: F14 · Poisson GLM with exposure offset
passages.text: (both sensors see the same activity in a stratum). It allows exposure to enter properly, so a cloudier month for one sensor is not read as lower sensitivity. And it extends naturally: day/night, view angle or season can be added as covariates without inventing a new method. It also clarifies a common confusion. With MODIS counts as the offset and only an intercept, the maximum-likelihood estimate of $e^{\beta}$ is exactly $\sum V/\sum M$. The GLM is then not an independent confirmation of the ratio of totals; it is the same

passages.source: F14 · Poisson GLM with exposure offset

The pipeline currently publishes the intercept-only form for each calendar month: k is total VIIRS over total MODIS cell-days across the overlap years. Fires come in bursts: a dry week, a harvest deadline or a ban lifted changes thousands of fields at once. A Poisson model assumes the spread of a count equals its mean, which real fire counts violate badly. The negative-binomial variance adds a second term that grows with the square of the mean. Every interval FIREWORK shows rests on a variance. If counts are assumed Poisson when they are bursty, bands on k and on harmonised values come out too narrow and readers believe the record is more certain than

harmonised values come out too narrow and readers believe the record is more certain than it is. Measuring dispersion on the real fit, and switching to the NB form when it is large, keeps the bands honest. The Validation page reports dispersion so that a reviewer can see why the intervals are as wide as they are. After fitting the count model (F14), the pipeline computes $\hat\phi$. Values near 1 support Poisson. Values above 1.5 trigger the NB family or a quasi-Poisson scale, which multiplies standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$. θ

passages.source: F16 · Delta-method interval for a ratio
passages.text: A quick formula gives the uncertainty of a ratio of two counts. It is exact only if the two counts are independent and Poisson. For two sensors watching the same fires neither holds, so FIREWORK shows this interval as an approximation and publishes the bootstrap band instead. Readers deserve a quick sense of precision, and the delta method is the one most textbooks teach. FIREWORK keeps it, labelled 'approx.', because seeing why it fails is instructive: the covariance term is positive (shared fires narrow the interval), while over-dispersion (F15) widens

The year-block bootstrap (F24) captures both without assuming either. With totals $V$ and $M$, the standard error of $\log k$ is $\sqrt{1/V + 1/M}$ under independence and the interval is $k\,e^{\pm 1.96\,\mathrm{se}}$. When either total is zero the formula is undefined and returns nothing; exact Poisson bounds (F26) apply to each count instead. passages.text: Is VIIRS simply a fixed multiple of MODIS, or does the multiple change with the size of the month? A power law lets the relation bend. FIREWORK decides between the two shapes by how well each predicts years it has not seen. If MODIS saturates in big fire months (many adjacent fires merge into one MODIS pixel while VIIRS still separates them), the true multiple would rise as months get bigger, and a single ratio would bias the harmonised peaks. If MODIS instead misses proportionally more in quiet months, the

passages.text: would bias the harmonised peaks. If MODIS instead misses proportionally more in quiet months, the multiple falls with size. A held-out comparison tells which shape the data support and by how much. For each overlap year: fit both models on the other years, predict the hidden year, and add up the Poisson deviance. The ratio model is the live calibration (one k per calendar month); the power law adds one parameter. If the power law improves held-out deviance by less than 2%, the simpler ratio is kept. Why does VIIRS see more fires? Because MODIS misses small ones. Matching fires that both satellites passed over within minutes, this curve gives the probability that MODIS detects a fire of a given strength, and the strength at which it detects half of them: FRP₅₀. The exchange rate k is a summary; this curve is the mechanism. It shows that k depends on the fire-size mix of a region and season: where fires are small (spring, winter, smallholder farms) MODIS misses more and k is larger; where fires are big,

(spring, winter, smallholder farms) MODIS misses more and k is larger; where fires are big, k is closer to 1. It also warns that k learned in one region may not transfer to another with different fires, which is why FIREWORK fits k per region and month. • Take S-NPP daytime detections with FRP on days when Aqua passed within 15 minutes.• For each, look for an Aqua detection within 1.5 km (MODIS geolocation and pixel size).• Fit a logistic regression of 'Aqua detected' on ln FRP of the VIIRS

pixel size).• Fit a logistic regression of 'Aqua detected' on ln FRP of the VIIRS fire.• Report FRP₅₀ = $e^{-\beta_0/\beta_1}$ and the curve. FRP is skewed (F21), so the logarithm is the natural scale: each doubling of strength adds the same amount to the log-odds. passages.text: When does the burning season open, peak and close? Within a declared window, the season starts when 10% of the window's detected activity has happened, ends at 90%, and peaks in the busiest week. These are dates of detected activity, which is what satellites can tell us. The challenge asks for the critical period of burning. Farmers, regulators and health agencies need to know whether the residue-burning season is arriving earlier or later and whether its end is moving into the colder weeks of November, when smoke traps more easily.

Is burning rising or falling over the years? The Mann–Kendall test counts, for every pair of years, whether the later one is higher or lower. It needs no straight line and no normal errors, which suits fire counts. A trend is the headline many users want: is stubble burning declining? Mann–Kendall answers on ranks, so one extreme year cannot manufacture a trend. Run on the harmonised series, it is not fooled by the 2012 jump, which a raw MODIS-then-VIIRS series would read as a large rise. Compute the sign of

which a raw MODIS-then-VIIRS series would read as a large rise. Compute the sign of every pairwise difference, sum, compute the variance with the tie correction, standardise with the continuity correction and read p. Fewer than eight years are reported as 'too short'. Autocorrelation is handled by F31 and the size of the trend by F32. The series shows why: it rises from 2,265 in 2001 (Terra only) to a plateau of 14,000–17,000 cell-days from 2005 to 2021, then falls steeply to 3,479 in 2025. Neighbouring years are often alike: a wet year follows a wet year, a policy lasts several seasons. That makes a series look more certain than it is. The Hamed–Rao correction inflates the variance of the Mann–Kendall score by the effective loss of independent years. Without it, a short positively autocorrelated series can show a 'significant' trend that is really a few long swings. The share of a site's detections that come from night passes separates the two, once it is adjusted for how many day and night looks the satellite had. passages.text: heading: A fire does not need to fill the pixel text: A 1 km MODIS pixel is one square kilometre, about 140 football fields. A burning field of rice stubble may cover only a few hundred square metres of that. The satellite records the average radiance of the whole pixel. Because the flame is thousands of times brighter at 4 µm, even a tiny burning fraction raises the average noticeably, while the 11 µm average hardly moves. heading: What the algorithm actually checks text: Both the MODIS (MOD14/MYD14) and VIIRS

passages.text: hardly moves. heading: What the algorithm actually checks text: Both the MODIS (MOD14/MYD14) and VIIRS 375 m algorithms run a similar sequence for every pixel. The exact thresholds differ between sensors, between day and night, and between versions; the logic is the same. Mask out water and cloud first. A cloudy pixel is labelled cloud, never 'no fire'. Absolute test: if the 4 µm brightness temperature is extremely high, the pixel is flagged as fire directly. Candidate test: the pixel must be warmer than usual at 4 µm and show

passages.text: directly. Candidate test: the pixel must be warmer than usual at 4 µm and show a large 4 µm minus 11 µm difference (ΔT). Contextual test: compare the candidate with valid neighbouring pixels in a window around it. It must stand out by several standard deviations in T4 and in ΔT. heading: Seeing the same thing in a satellite image text: A true-colour image (red, green, blue bands) shows smoke but rarely flames. Cell-days ask a simpler, steadier question: was there fire in this place on this day? heading: How a point finds its cell text: row = floor((lat + 90) ÷ 0.1) and col = floor((lon + 180)

Volcanoes, gas flares and steel plants must be removed before a crop-burning calendar makes sense. hinglish: Har garam pixel khet ki aag nahi hota — factory, gas flare, jwalamukhi bhi chamakte hain. certainly industrial. title: Season text: Punjab paddy residue burns Oct–Nov, wheat residue Apr–May; forest fires follow dry seasons. figures: satellite: src: /learn/sat/punjab_721_2020-11-04.webp caption: MODIS Terra bands 7-2-1 false colour, same area and day. id: lesson-10 num: 10 title: Fire power and smoke kicker: FRP, energy and what reaches the air lead: Fire Radiative Power (FRP, in megawatts) measures how fast a fire is releasing radiant energy at the moment of the pass. Adding FRP over time gives Fire Radiative Energy, which scales with the amount of vegetation burned and so with the smoke released. It is the bridge from fire detection to air quality. hinglish: FRP = aag kitni zor se jal rahi hai (MW). Zyada FRP = zyada dhuan, lekin ek pixel

kitni zor se jal rahi hai (MW). Zyada FRP = zyada dhuan, lekin ek pixel ka total hai, ek aag ka nahi. points: title: Units text: FRP in MW per pixel; Fire Radiative Energy (FRE) in MJ = FRP integrated over time. title: Biomass link text: Studies find roughly 0.37 kg of dry matter burned per MJ of FRE (Wooster et al. 2005), with large uncertainty. title: Sensor differences text: VIIRS sees weaker fires and has smaller pixels, so its per-pixel FRP is lower (Lesson 02). title: Snapshots only text:

has smaller pixels, so its per-pixel FRP is lower (Lesson 02). title: Snapshots only text: Two looks a day cannot integrate a fire that flares between passes; FRE from polar orbiters is a rough estimate. figures: src: /learn/fig/l2_frp.webp caption: FRP per pixel in the live feed: VIIRS reaches weaker fires (lower median) than MODIS. Because emission rises steeply with temperature, the 4 µm excess is roughly proportional to the total radiated power, regardless of exact fire temperature. heading: From power to smoke text: Integrate FRP over the life of a fire to get energy, convert energy to

text: Integrate FRP over the life of a fire to get energy, convert energy to burned biomass, and multiply by emission factors (grams of PM2.5, CO or CO₂ per kg burned) to estimate emissions. Each step adds uncertainty. heading: Air quality next to fire text: FIREWORK can show OpenAQ PM2.5 and PM10 from ground stations beside the fire record. Smoke travels with the wind, so a station's peak can lag the fire and be hundreds of kilometres away. heading: Common mistake text: Comparing raw FRP across sensors or across swath

Confidence 0.6 ≠ 60%. points: title: More dots = more fire text: More dots can mean a finer sensor, more satellite passes or fewer clouds. title: No detection = no fire text: Under cloud or between passes it means unknown. title: Burned area validates hotspots text: MCD64A1 burned area uses MODIS active fire as an input, so it is not independent. title: Confidence 0.6 means 60 % text: VIIRS classes l/n/h are categories; MODIS 0–100 is a score, not a probability. figures: src: /learn/fig/myth_confidence.webp caption: Confidence values in

The number of fire pixels depends on at least four things besides fire: pixel size (VIIRS 375 m vs MODIS 1 km), the number of satellite passes (one MODIS vs two MODIS vs three VIIRS satellites), cloud and smoke, and view angle. In the live feed for 2026-10-30 → 2026-11-02, VIIRS S-NPP alone reported 73,292 pixels while MODIS reported 12,511, over the same fires. heading: Myth 2 — “No detection = no fire” text: A cell with no fire pixels was either clear and not burning, or not observed: cloud-covered,

cell with no fire pixels was either clear and not burning, or not observed: cloud-covered, smoke-covered, between overpasses, or the fire was too small or too cool. The fire mask records cloud explicitly so we can tell these apart. FIREWORK shows unobserved cells as null with a status, never 0. heading: Myth 3 — “Burned area validates hotspots” text: The MODIS burned-area product MCD64A1 maps burn scars from changes in surface reflectance, but it uses MODIS active-fire detections to train and seed its classification. If you check hotspots against MCD64A1

MODIS active-fire detections to train and seed its classification. If you check hotspots against MCD64A1 and they agree, part of that agreement is built in. It is a useful companion product, not an independent judge. Independent checks use higher-resolution imagery (Landsat, Sentinel-2), field reports or airborne data. heading: Myth 4 — “Confidence 0.6 means 60 %” text: VIIRS labels each detection low (l), nominal (n) or high (h). These are categories describing which tests the pixel passed and how strongly, not probabilities. MODIS gives a 0–100 confidence score; FIRMS suggests

pixel passed and how strongly, not probabilities. MODIS gives a 0–100 confidence score; FIRMS suggests reading 0–29 as low, 30–79 as nominal, 80–100 as high. A score of 60 is not a 60 % chance of fire, and VIIRS 'n' cannot be converted to a number. heading: Three more pitfalls text: A hotspot is a pixel, not a fire: one large fire makes many pixels; several small fires can share one pixel. A cell-day is not burned area: it says some fire was detected in a grid cell on a

not burned area: it says some fire was detected in a grid cell on a day, not how many hectares burned. Harmonised values are estimates with a band, not measurements. pdf suggested: /learn/pdf/FIREWORK_Learn_13_myths.pdf

NASA INTERNATIONAL SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026 · CHALLENGE: HARMONIZATION OF MODIS AND VIIRS HOT SPOTS FIREWORK CHRONOS: Harmonising a Quarter- Century of MODIS and VIIRS Active-Fire Detections into a Comparable Burning Calendar Formulation, estimators, uncertainty, validation design and first results on the global archive and on Punjab–Haryana, India Dhruv Sharma and Team FIREWORK Research report · November 2026 · Correspondence: github.com/Dhruvsharma-DSAS/SpaceCode- ABSTRACT NASA's record of satellite active-fire detections began with MODIS on Terra (November 2000) and Aqua (July 2002) and continued with VIIRS on Suomi NPP from January 2012. The

and Aqua (July 2002) and continued with VIIRS on Suomi NPP from January 2012. The two instruments differ in pixel size (≈1 km versus 375 m), overpass time, cloud masking and processing, so their detection counts are not directly comparable. Joined naively, the global record of fire cell-days jumps by a factor of 2.31 in 2012 (1.98 M in 2011 to 4.57 M in 2012), although no physical change in burning occurred. The problem is now urgent: Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data on 2 November 2026 and NASA plans

now urgent: Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data on 2 November 2026 and NASA plans to end Terra and Aqua MODIS science in 2027, so the overlap period that makes calibration possible is closing. We present FIREWORK CHRONOS, a method for producing a month-by-year burning calendar for any area on Earth on one common scale. Detections are reduced to fire cell-days on a 0.1° grid in local solar time; a sensor exchange rate is estimated per calendar month from the 2012–2025 overlap as a ratio of totals, which equals the

per calendar month from the 2012–2025 overlap as a ratio of totals, which equals the maximum-likelihood estimate of an exposure-offset Poisson model; MODIS-era months are expressed as VIIRS-equivalent values with a 95% year-block bootstrap band. Three further layers an- notate, but never alter, this calendar: source attribution with abstention, a detection-timing diagnostic, and robust anomaly and trend statistics. We audit 46 formulas, declare twelve validation gates before any real-data run, and report first results. Global monthly ranges from 2.13 (July) to 3.10 (February). On held-out years the method meets its

monthly ranges from 2.13 (July) to 3.10 (February). On held-out years the method meets its pre-declared accuracy gate (median relative error 9.7% against a 15% limit) and removes about four-fifths of the 2012 step across 3,081 regional series (seam ratio 0.19 against a 0.25 limit). In Punjab–Haryana, harmonised October–November activity shows no significant trend in 2003–2016 (Mann–Kendall ) but a significant decline in 2016–2025 ( ; Sen slope −1,400 cell-days per year). We show why this decline must be read together with independent evidence that burn- ing has shifted to

this decline must be read together with independent evidence that burn- ing has shifted to late afternoon, after the satellite overpasses. Keywords: active fire; MODIS; VIIRS; sensor harmonisation; inter-calibration; fire cell-days; exposure; block bootstrap; Mann–Kendall; crop-residue burning; Punjab 1. Introduction Satellite active-fire products are the only consistent, global, daily record of where and when vegetation and other fires burn. NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) distributes detections from MODIS Collection 6.1 (from 1 November 2000) and from the VIIRS 375 m product on Suomi NPP (from 20 January

November 2000) and from the VIIRS 375 m product on Suomi NPP (from 20 January 2012), NOAA-20 (from 1 April 2018) and NOAA-21 (from 1 March 2023) [1–4]. Responders, scientists, land managers and air-quality agencies use these detections to answer a simple question: is this season's burning higher or lower than usual, and is it changing over time? Answering that question across the whole record is not simple. The MODIS and VIIRS instruments see the same fires differently. VIIRS has a nadir pixel roughly seven times smaller in area than

same fires differently. VIIRS has a nadir pixel roughly seven times smaller in area than MODIS, so it detects many small fires that MODIS misses [2, 3]. The satellites cross the equator at different local k k p = 0.32 p = 0.007 FIREWORK CHRONOS · Harmonising MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records NASA Space Apps 2026 1 / 20

times, their orbits drift, clouds remove different observations for each sensor, and the algorithms and confidence scales differ. A burning calendar built by concatenating MODIS before 2012 and VIIRS after- wards therefore contains an artificial step — the 2012 seam — and any trend test applied to it will re- port a spurious increase. The timing of this work matters. NASA has announced that Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data on 2 November 2026, that Terra MODIS science ends in February 2027 and that Aqua MODIS science ends in September

Terra MODIS science ends in February 2027 and that Aqua MODIS science ends in September 2027 [5, 6]. The 2012–2026 overlap, when both instruments observed the same fires, is the only period from which the two records can be tied together. Once MODIS ends, the overlap can no longer be extended. The European CAMS Global Fire Assimilation System began adding VIIRS along- side MODIS in December 2025 for the same reason [7]. The problem also has a direct human dimension. In the Indian states of Punjab and Haryana, post-har- vest

has a direct human dimension. In the Indian states of Punjab and Haryana, post-har- vest burning of rice residue in October and November contributes to severe winter air pollution in Delhi and the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Officially reported active-fire counts in Punjab have fallen sharply since 2021, yet secondary reporting of the iFOREST Stubble Burning Status Report 2025 indicates that burned area fell much less (≈31,447 km² in 2022 to ≈20,000 km² in 2025) and that more than 90% of large farm fires in 2024–25 occurred after 15:00 local time, compared

more than 90% of large farm fires in 2024–25 occurred after 15:00 local time, compared with about 3% in 2021 [8, 9]. If true, a count-only calendar would describe a collapse in burning that did not happen. A harmonised cal- endar must therefore be honest about what the satellites cannot see. Contributions. This report makes five contributions: 1. A precise problem statement and estimand for a comparable burning calendar (Section 2), separat- ing detections, cell-days, exposure rates and burned area. 2. A complete, audited formula set (46 formulas in seven

exposure rates and burned area. 2. Conclusion The 25-year satellite fire record can be made comparable, but only if the comparison is defined carefully and its limits are stated. FIREWORK CHRONOS reduces MODIS and VIIRS detections to fire cell- days on a common 0.1° grid in local solar time, estimates a monthly exchange rate from the 2012–2025 overlap and expresses the MODIS era on the

a monthly exchange rate from the 2012–2025 overlap and expresses the MODIS era on the VIIRS scale with a bootstrap interval. On real data the method passes its pre-declared held-out accuracy gate (9.7% median error) and removes about four- fifths of the 2012 seam across 3,081 regional series. Global VIIRS/MODIS exchange rates of 2.1–3.1, and regional rates up to about 6, show why a single constant is not sufficient. In Punjab–Haryana, the har- monised record shows a sharp post-2016 decline in detected burning; because burning has reportedly moved to hours

shows a sharp post-2016 decline in detected burning; because burning has reportedly moved to hours that no polar-orbiting satellite observes, the calendar reports that decline together with a timing flag rather than as proof that burning has ended. With Suomi NPP data delivery ended and MODIS ending in 2027, building this bridge now is what keeps the 25-year record usable after MODIS.
